transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you too. Well... I suppose I'm here because things at work have gotten really complicated lately. I work as a cashier—which, you know, I have a bachelor's degree, so it's not exactly where I thought I'd be at 54, but a job is a job, right? You have to pay the bills. But lately, well, I came in because when I'm standing at the register, I keep getting... stuck. I just get stuck doing these things that absolutely don't fit the moment. 

Like, I'll be ringing someone's groceries up, and instead of just sliding the can of soup or whatever across the glass, I start tapping the scanner. And it's not just a random tap, I have to tap it in this specific pattern, and I just keep doing it instead of scanning. Or, even worse, it happens when I'm making change. The register drawer will pop open, and I'll reach down to grab the fives or the ones, and my hand just stops. It completely freezes right over the cash drawer. I'll just be standing there, completely still, hovering over the money, and the customer is just standing there staring at me, waiting for their change. You know how people get at the store, they start shifting their weight, sighing, clearing their throats because they're in a hurry... and I know they're waiting, but I just stay frozen there. 

It's been causing a lot of problems, obviously, because the lines get backed up. And, well, last week it finally got me written up. My manager pulled me off the floor and took me into the back office and actually put a formal warning in my file about it. He said I was holding up the flow of the store, which I understand, but I just can't seem to stop getting stuck like that. So... I guess that's what brings me in.

When you find yourself tapping the scanner or freezing over the cash drawer, do you feel an internal urge or a sense of 'must' that you are trying to satisfy, or does it feel more like your body is simply not obeying your commands?

Well, that's the thing, Dr. Smith, it's not like an itch I have to scratch, if that makes sense. It's not like I'm standing there thinking, "Oh, I really need to tap this scanner right now, I just have to do it." It's nothing like that at all. It's more like... well, like my body just decides to do its own thing, completely independent of what I actually want to be doing, which is scanning the soup and getting the customer out of my line. 

I'll be standing there, looking right at the can of soup, knowing exactly what I'm supposed to do, and my hand just starts doing the tapping pattern. Tap, tap, tap-tap. Just like that. And I'm in my head going, "What are we doing? Stop tapping, scan the soup," but my hand just keeps going. And the freezing, oh, the freezing is exactly the same. I'll see the five-dollar bill in the drawer, I'll know the customer needs five dollars and thirty-two cents in change, I reach down, and then... nothing. It's like the connection between my brain and my arm just gets severed right at the elbow. I'm telling my hand to grab the bill, I'm practically screaming at it in my head because I can hear the customer sighing and shifting their weight, but my hand just hovers there. It's completely stuck. 

It's so frustrating because I know it doesn't fit the moment. I know it's completely inappropriate for a cashier to just stand there frozen like a statue or tapping on the glass while a line of six people is waiting. And my manager, well, he doesn't understand it either, which is why he wrote me up last week. He thinks I'm just spacing out or not paying attention, but I am paying attention! I'm acutely aware of everything happening, I just can't make my body cooperate with the situation. So, no, it's not an urge at all. It's just... getting stuck, plain and simple.
Have you noticed any other physical changes lately, such as your movements feeling generally slower, your muscles feeling stiff, or any shaking in your hands when you are at rest?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I haven't noticed anything like that. It's not like I'm moving through molasses all day, you know? My walking is fine, my general movements are fine. I'm not shuffling around the store or anything. And stiffness? No, my muscles feel perfectly normal, really. I mean, I'm 54, so I get the occasional ache if I sleep wrong or if I'm on my feet for an eight-hour shift without a good break—which happens more often than it should at the store, let me tell you, because they are always understaffed. But it's just normal soreness, not like a rigid stiffness or anything out of the ordinary. 

And as for shaking... no, definitely not. My hands are completely steady when I'm just sitting or resting. Even when I'm holding a cup of coffee in the breakroom, there's no tremor, no shaking at all. It's just the freezing and the tapping when I'm actually trying to do something specific at the register. When I'm just sitting at home watching TV or reading, my body is perfectly still and relaxed. It's so strange, isn't it? That it only happens in those specific moments at work, but the rest of the time, I feel physically completely normal. So, no slowness, no stiffness, no shaking. Just... the getting stuck.
Have you experienced any other unusual symptoms, such as recurring headaches, changes in your vision, or moments where you felt confused or lost track of where you were?

Headaches? No, no, I wouldn't say I have recurring headaches. I mean, sure, if I skip my morning coffee—which I really try not to do, because I have this specific routine, you know, I brew a pot at 6:00 AM sharp before my shift—I might get a little dull ache right behind my eyes, but that's just normal caffeine withdrawal, isn't it? It's certainly not a recurring, unusual medical headache. The fluorescent lights at the supermarket can be a bit much sometimes, they have this constant, annoying hum and they're so aggressively bright, but they don't give me headaches. 

And my vision is perfectly fine, too. I haven't noticed any blurriness or dark spots or anything like that. I can read the tiny print on the coupons people bring in—and let me tell you, people bring in these crumpled up, faded coupons from three months ago and expect me to honor them, so I have to read the expiration dates very carefully. If my vision was going bad, I'd definitely notice it there, but my eyes are doing just fine. 

And as for feeling confused or losing track of where I am... no, absolutely not. Never. That's actually the most maddening part of this whole situation with the register, Dr. Smith. I am completely, one hundred percent aware of my surroundings. I know exactly where I am—I know I'm at register four, I know it's Tuesday afternoon, I know the manager, Greg, is probably watching me from the front office window. I don't lose time, and I certainly don't get confused about what I'm doing. When my hand is hovering over that cash drawer, I know exactly what the money is, I know the math, I know who the change belongs to. I'm just trapped there watching it happen. If I were confused, well, maybe it wouldn't be so incredibly embarrassing, you know? If I was just lost in a daydream or forgot where I was, I could excuse it. But I'm not. I'm fully present, my mind is completely sharp. So, no, none of those things you mentioned. My head is clear, my eyes are fine, and I know exactly where I am at all times. It really is just this bizarre thing with my hands getting stuck.
Have you or those close to you noticed any recent changes in your personality, such as becoming more irritable, impulsive, or struggling to follow social norms in ways you didn't before?

Changes in my personality? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I'm the exact same person I've always been. If I were becoming irritable or impulsive, believe me, I wouldn't last a single shift at the store. Being a cashier, especially at a busy supermarket where people are tired and just want to get home, you have to have the patience of a saint. You really do. 

Just the other day, for example, I had a woman come through my line—this was right in the middle of the evening rush, mind you, lines backing up into the aisles—and she wanted to argue with me over a twenty-cent difference on a can of diced tomatoes. Twenty cents! And she was getting quite loud and condescending about it. Now, if I were irritable or impulsive, or if I was losing my grip on how to behave socially, that would be the perfect time to snap, wouldn't it? To just tell her to pay the difference or leave the store. But I didn't do anything like that. I just smiled, apologized for the confusion, called Greg over to do a price override, and waited patiently. I didn't raise my voice, I didn't get angry. I followed all the customer service protocols to the letter, just like I always do. 

And as for social norms, well, I've always been a very polite, rule-following kind of guy. I have my bachelor's degree, I know how to conduct myself in a professional and public setting. I say 'please' and 'thank you,' I hold the door for people, I make polite small talk about the weather when I'm ringing up the groceries. I don't just blurt things out or act inappropriately. Even my sister, who calls me every single Sunday evening without fail, hasn't said a word about me acting differently. We just talk about her garden and my week, same as always. If I were acting strange or being short with her, she would be the first one to tell me, believe me, she never holds back. 

So, really, my personality is completely intact. My mood is fine, my temper is perfectly under control. It's just... like I said, it's just this incredibly frustrating thing with my body freezing up or tapping at the register. But inside? In my mind and my personality and the way I treat people? I'm exactly the same guy I was ten years ago.
Does this 'freezing' or 'tapping' ever happen when you are performing repetitive, precise movements at home, such as when you are typing on a computer, cooking, or working on a hobby?

Well, at home? No, not at all. That’s what makes this whole thing so incredibly baffling to me. I mean, I do plenty of precise things at my house. I cook dinner for myself every single night—I make this very involved vegetable lasagna from scratch where I have to chop the zucchini and the onions into these perfectly uniform little cubes. It's very repetitive, very precise knife work, you know? And my hands never freeze up when I’m holding the chef’s knife. Never. And typing, too! I type long emails to my sister on my laptop, my fingers just flying across the keys, and I never get stuck on a letter or tap a key in a weird rhythm. Everything works exactly the way it's supposed to. 

But then I go to work, and... well, that’s exactly why I came in to see you. Because at the register, I just keep getting stuck doing things that completely don’t fit the moment. It’s like my body just derails right in the middle of a transaction. I’ll be ringing someone up, and instead of moving the groceries down the belt, I'm suddenly tapping the scanner in a pattern. Just tapping the plastic side of it, over and over in this specific rhythm, while the items are just piling up. 

Or, even worse, I’ll have the till open to give someone their change, and I just freeze. I completely freeze with my hand hovering right over the cash drawer. The money is right there, I know exactly what bills to pull, but the customer is just standing there waiting, looking at me like I’ve lost my mind, and I'm just stuck hovering there. It doesn't fit the situation at all, it's so out of place. And it’s really starting to become a serious problem, because last week, it actually got me written up. Greg pulled me into the back office because a customer complained that I was just standing there like a statue holding up the evening rush. He handed me this formal warning on official company letterhead—which I’ve never had in my entire life, I have a spotless employment record—just because I keep getting stuck like that. So, no, it never happens when I'm chopping vegetables or typing at home. It's just at that register.
When you are at the register and these episodes occur, do you feel any specific emotional distress or anxiety immediately before or during the moment you get stuck?

Well, let me think about that. Anxiety... distress... no. No, I really wouldn't say that I do. It’s not like a panic attack or anything of that sort, if that’s what you’re getting at. I mean, I’ve seen people have panic attacks—my old roommate back when I was getting my degree used to get them right before finals, his face would go completely pale and he'd say he couldn't breathe—but this is absolutely nothing like that. 

There’s really no warning sign, no buildup of nerves, no racing heart or sweaty palms or anything. I could be having a completely pleasant, entirely routine interaction. Just a few days ago, for instance, I was ringing up Mrs. Gable. She comes in every Monday and Thursday, always buys the same brand of peppermint tea and a loaf of the bakery sourdough, and we were having a perfectly lovely chat about the humidity we've been having lately. I was completely calm, completely relaxed, just reaching out to take her store loyalty card. And then... well, my hand just stopped. It just hovered there right in the space between us. 

And during the actual moment? While I'm stuck there or while I'm tapping the scanner? I wouldn't call it distress, exactly. It's certainly not anxiety. It's more just... well, it's just this profound sense of being disconnected from the movement. I'm looking at my hand, and I'm looking at the customer, and my brain is saying 'take the card, swipe the card, finish the transaction,' but the hand just doesn't obey. I'm completely calm in my head while it's happening. I'm just... waiting for the connection to re-establish, I guess you could say. 

Now, obviously, it's only *after* the fact, or when it drags on too long and the customer starts clearing their throat or waving their hand in front of my face like I'm deaf, that I start to feel embarrassed and frustrated. And when Greg pulls me into the back office to give me a written warning, yes, of course that's incredibly distressing. But right before it happens? Or right in the exact moment I get stuck? No, there’s no anxiety at all. It’s completely out of the blue. I’m just doing my job one second, completely at ease, and the next second my body just hits the brakes. So, no, I can't say I feel any sort of emotional trigger or panic with it at all.
Have you ever experienced any periods where you lost track of who you are, or found yourself in a place or situation with no memory of how you got there?

Lost track of who I am? Oh, no. No, no, definitely not. I mean, my memory is sharp as a tack, it really is. I've never just... woken up somewhere and not known how I got there. That sounds completely terrifying, honestly, like something out of a late-night movie, but no, that has never once happened to me. 

I have a very, very structured routine, you see. I know exactly where I am every single minute of the day. I wake up every morning at exactly 6:15, I brew my coffee—just a standard drip, nothing fancy, but I do buy these specific medium-roast beans from a little shop two blocks over—and then I walk down to the corner to catch the 42 bus at 7:05 so I can get to the supermarket by 7:45 for my shift. I never deviate from that. I don't wander off, I don't lose time. 

Even when those... those freezing episodes happen at the register, the ones we were just talking about? I know exactly who I am and exactly where I am the entire time. I know I'm standing at register four, I know my name tag is pinned straight on my apron, I know I'm ringing up groceries. My mind doesn't go blank, and I certainly don't forget my own identity. I've been the exact same person my whole life. I have my bachelor's degree in history, I've lived in the same apartment for twelve years, I pay my rent on the first of the month without fail. I remember all of it. 

I remember conversations I had weeks ago, too. Like I said, my sister calls me every Sunday, and I can tell you exactly what we talked about last week—she's having a terrible time with aphids on her rose bushes this year, just awful, and we spent a good twenty minutes discussing whether neem oil or ladybugs would be the better solution. So, no, my memory and my sense of self are completely, one hundred percent intact. I never lose track of time or end up in strange places, not ever. It's just my hands that stop cooperating sometimes, never my mind.
Can you recall if anything particularly stressful, upsetting, or physically traumatic happened in your life right around the time these episodes at the register first began?

Stressful? Upsetting? Well, let me really think back on that. If I look at the calendar and try to retrace my steps... the voices and the more clearly out-of-place moments have been happening for about the last three months. Yes, right around three months. I know that for a fact because it was right at the tail end of our quarterly inventory at the supermarket. 

Now, inventory week is always a bit of a headache, I won't lie to you. Management gets incredibly fussy, we have to count every single item on the floor, every can of soup, every box of pasta, and Greg is always pacing up and down the aisles with his clipboard looking like the world is ending. But for me? No, it wasn't traumatic in the slightest. I've done dozens of inventories in my time there. It's just counting. It's just part of the retail cycle. 

So, no, there were no car accidents, no head injuries, nobody died. I didn't have a terrible breakup or get evicted. My life was exactly as it always is, perfectly structured. I was taking my 42 bus, brewing my medium-roast coffee, paying my rent on time. But that three-month mark is definitely when everything shifted. It was a Tuesday, I believe, and I was ringing up a customer who was buying ingredients for what looked like a massive batch of chili—lots of kidney beans, tomato paste, onions—and that's when it all really started. The voices chiming in, and then those moments where my hand just decides to stop working and hover over the scanner or tap against the plastic. They both just sort of arrived together, about three months ago, and they've been with me every single shift since. But as for a big, dramatic, upsetting event that kicked it all off? No, I really can't say there was one. It was just a perfectly ordinary week.
You mentioned 'the voices' a moment ago; could you tell me more about what you mean by that?

Well, yes, the voices. I suppose I did mention that just now, didn't I? It’s... well, it’s really quite strange, to be perfectly honest with you, and it happens on most days now. 

I'll just be standing there at register four—which is my usual register, right next to the floral department, so it always smells faintly of lilies and that crinkly plastic wrap they use—and I'll hear what sounds exactly like a couple of people talking. Not whispering, mind you, but talking at a perfectly normal conversational volume, just... just right off to the side of me. Just slightly out of my peripheral vision. 

Sometimes it's just my name. I'll hear them calling for me, clear as day, sounding like it's coming all the way from the back stockroom. Like they need me to come off the register and help unload a pallet or something. But other times—and this is the part that really gets under my skin, honestly—they'll be commenting on my actual work. They'll say I rang something up wrong. I'll be scanning a carton of eggs or a bag of flour, and I'll hear them say, 'He missed the barcode on that,' or 'He charged her for the organic apples instead of the regular ones, he's messing it all up.' 

And of course, when you hear someone criticizing your work right over your shoulder, you turn around. That's just a natural human reaction. So I'll stop what I'm doing and I'll spin around to see who's standing there critiquing my scanning technique, fully expecting to see Greg or one of the shift leads... but there’s absolutely nobody there. Just the empty magazine racks and the chewing gum display. 

And the really baffling part is that no one else reacts. I'll look over at the customer I'm ringing up, or I'll glance over at Cindy who usually works register three, just to see if they heard who was talking, but they're just going about their business. They didn't hear a single thing. Not a peep. The customer is just fishing around in her purse for exact change, completely oblivious. I even asked Greg about it once, asked if corporate had installed some sort of new intercom system or hidden speakers for loss prevention that might be picking up radio interference, but he just looked at me like I had two heads. So yes, it's just these two voices, talking away, and nobody else seems to have the faintest idea they're even speaking. It's incredibly distracting, as you can imagine.

When you hear these voices, do they sound as if they are coming from inside your own head, or do they sound like they are coming from the space around you, just like the voice of a real person standing nearby?

Oh, outside. Definitely outside. Not in my head at all, no. I mean, if it were inside my head, it would just sound like my own thoughts, wouldn't it? Like when you're silently reciting a grocery list or trying to remember the capital of a state, you know that's coming from inside. But this isn't like that at all. 

Like I was just saying, most days I hear what sounds exactly like a couple of real, physical people talking just off to the side of me. It has... well, it has distance to it, if that makes sense. Spatial depth. When I hear them calling my name from the stockroom, it sounds exactly like a voice traveling fifty feet down the aisles, bouncing off the linoleum floors and the metal shelving. It echoes the way a real voice would echo in a large retail space. And then when they're right behind me, saying I rang something up wrong—like the organic apples I mentioned earlier—it sounds like they are standing maybe two feet away. Just over my right shoulder, usually. It sounds exactly like the voice of a real person standing right there in the physical space of the store, speaking directly into my ear. 

That's exactly why I always turn around! Because my ears are telling me, with absolute certainty, that a human being has just spoken into the air right next to me. But then I turn, and... well, there's nobody there. Just the magazines. And like I said, no one else heard it. If it were just a thought in my head, I wouldn't expect Cindy on register three to hear it, obviously. But because it sounds so incredibly real, so out loud and in the room, it just completely baffles me that the customers don't even blink. 

I actually spent a good twenty minutes on my lunch break last Thursday inspecting the ceiling tiles and the air conditioning vents above register four, just trying to see if maybe sound was traveling through the ductwork from the breakroom. Because in my apartment building, you see, the vents carry sound perfectly from the floor below—I can hear my neighbor's television clear as day through my bathroom vent—so I thought maybe it was an architectural quirk of the supermarket. But no, I couldn't find anything. It's just... they sound completely real and completely outside of me, but nobody else hears a single word.
When these voices are commenting on your work or talking near you, do they ever tell you to perform those specific tapping motions or to freeze in place?

Tell me to do the tapping? Oh, no, no, not at all. They aren't giving me instructions or orders or anything of that sort. It’s not like a director in a play telling me where to stand or what to do with my hands. 

Like I was saying just a moment ago, it’s really just those couple of people talking off to the side of me. Most days, it's exactly what I described—they might be calling my name all the way from the back stockroom, dragging out the vowels, or they're just hovering there right over my shoulder, critiquing me. They'll say I rang up the wrong item, or that I'm messing up the transaction, just going on and on about my performance at the register. But they never say, 'Hey, freeze right there,' or 'Tap your hand on the scanner.' It’s more like... well, it’s more like I'm the subject of their conversation, rather than them trying to boss me around. 

The tapping and the freezing, those moments where my hand just sort of stops and hovers over the plastic, that just seems to happen on its own. It's completely separate from what the voices are actually saying, even if they both started around the same time three months ago. It's incredibly frustrating, really, because I’ll be in the middle of bagging someone's groceries, I'll hear these people talking about how I'm doing it all wrong, and I'll spin around to catch them in the act, fully prepared to give them a piece of my mind... and there is just absolutely nobody there. Just thin air. And the customer is just staring at me, maybe tapping their credit card on the counter, completely deaf to the fact that someone was just standing there loudly criticizing my scanning! 

It honestly makes you feel like you're the only one in the room paying any attention to your surroundings. But no, to answer your question, they don't command me to do the physical motions. They just talk, and critique, and then vanish the second I turn my head.

You mentioned these voices and the freezing episodes began about three months ago; have you ever experienced any similar symptoms, like hearing voices or feeling like your body was not obeying you, at any point in your life before those three months?

Before three months ago? Oh, no. No, never. That’s what makes this whole situation so incredibly baffling to me, to be perfectly honest. I’m fifty-four years old, I have my bachelor’s degree, I’ve held down steady work my entire adult life, and I can tell you with absolute certainty that for the first fifty-three and three-quarters years of my life, my surroundings were perfectly normal. Well, you know, normal in the sense that if I heard someone talking, there was an actual human being standing there moving their lips. 

I never heard anyone calling my name from empty stockrooms or critiquing my scanning technique when no one was there. And my body, too—it always did exactly what I told it to do. If I wanted to pick up a can of soup and drag it across the barcode reader, my hand just did it. There was no hesitation, no freezing in mid-air like a wind-up toy that’s suddenly run out of tension in its spring. 

So, no, I’ve never experienced anything even remotely like this in the past. The voices and the more clearly out-of-place moments, like the freezing up, they have been happening for about the last three months, and only the last three months. I actually remember exactly when it started because it was right around the time the store management put up those big promotional displays for the summer grilling season—you know, those giant, flimsy cardboard cutouts of the hamburgers and hot dogs that always get knocked over by the oversized shopping carts because people don't know how to turn corners properly. 

Before those displays went up, I was perfectly fine. I was the most reliable cashier on the floor. I'd just ring people up, ask if they found everything alright, print the receipt, and that was that. A perfectly smooth transaction every time. To just suddenly have these two people narrating my supposed mistakes out of thin air, and my hands just stopping over the register for no earthly reason... it’s entirely new. It just started out of the blue roughly ninety days ago, right there next to the lilies in the floral department, and it hasn't stopped since. You'd think there would be some sort of warning sign, or maybe it would build up over years and years, but no. Just three months of this... this constant, baffling interruption to my day.
Has anyone in your immediate or extended family ever struggled with similar experiences, such as hearing voices or having their body move in ways they didn't intend?

In my family? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, if they did, they certainly never breathed a word of it to me or anyone else, not even at the Thanksgiving table after a few glasses of wine. 

My family is... well, we're a very practical, very grounded bunch, I suppose you could say. My father, for instance, he worked in logistics for a regional shipping company for thirty-five years. He was a very by-the-numbers sort of man. He never heard anything that wasn't physically there in the room with him. If he heard a voice, it was because someone was standing right in front of his desk handing him a clipboard or a shipping manifest. And my mother, she taught middle school history for decades, so she was always extremely focused on facts and dates and reality. She passed away about ten years ago, but I can tell you she was sharp as a tack right up until the very end. She never once froze up or stared off into space, except maybe when she was trying to remember if she'd left the oven on, but that's just a normal thing people do, isn't it? 

Even if you look at my extended family—I have an uncle out in Ohio who used to sell insurance, and a couple of cousins I still exchange Christmas cards with every December—none of them have ever mentioned anything remotely like this. We just don't have this sort of... this sort of strangeness in our bloodline, as far as I know. Everyone just goes to work, does their jobs, pays their taxes, and goes to sleep. 

That's honestly a big part of why I'm so incredibly baffled by all of this! It’s like I’m the only one in the entire history of my family who has ever had to deal with invisible people critiquing their bagging skills while they're just trying to earn a paycheck. If my grandfather or my great-aunt had ever experienced something like their hands just stopping in mid-air for no earthly reason, I’m absolutely sure there would be some sort of family lore about it, you know? Some hushed whispers at family reunions or a cautionary tale passed down. But there’s just nothing. We are, historically speaking, boringly normal. So, no, I really don't have anything to give you on that front. I don't think there's any family connection here at all.
During these episodes where you freeze, have you ever found that your body remains in the position you were placed in, or that you can be moved by someone else like a mannequin?

Like a mannequin? Well... I mean, I don't think so. Honestly, no one has ever stepped up and tried to just grab my arm and reposition me while it's happening. I mean, can you imagine a customer just reaching across the conveyor belt to move my arm? That would be a complete violation of personal space. 

But the freezing itself, and these other movements, they are exactly why I came in to see you in the first place. Because at the register, I just keep getting stuck doing things that absolutely do not fit the moment. It’s not just standing still. Sometimes I get stuck tapping the scanner in a pattern. Just... tap, tap, pause, tap, right on the glass where the laser comes out, over and over in this specific rhythm, completely ignoring the groceries piling up. Or, like I mentioned, the freezing—I'll just freeze completely solid with my hand hovering right over the open cash drawer. I'll have the customer's change literally inches from my fingers, and my hand just stops dead, and I'm stuck there while the customer is waiting and staring at me, probably wondering if I'm trying to steal their money or if I'm just incredibly rude. 

It's completely inappropriate for the middle of a transaction, and it's entirely out of my control. And the worst part, the absolute worst part, is that last week it actually got me written up. My manager, Brenda—who usually puts me on register four because I’m so reliable—pulled me into the back office next to the breakroom and handed me a formal written warning for 'unprofessional delays' and odd behavior on the floor. Fifty-four years old, a bachelor's degree, decades of perfect employment, and I'm getting written up because my hand decides to tap out a rhythm on a barcode scanner or freeze like a statue over a pile of five-dollar bills! So, no, nobody is posing me like a doll, but my body is certainly getting stuck doing things it has absolutely no business doing right in the middle of my shift.
I know you mentioned your family is very grounded, but has anyone in your family ever been diagnosed with schizophrenia, psychosis, or any condition involving a break from reality?

No, no, definitely not. I mean, if you're asking for an official diagnosis of... well, of any of those things you just named, the answer is absolutely zero. I’ve actually been racking my brain about this lately, trying to trace back through the family tree, you know, just to see if maybe there was some great-uncle or a second cousin who was, I don't know, hidden away or had some sort of "nervous breakdown" back in the fifties that nobody talked about, but there is just nothing. 

My parents... well, like I was saying before, my dad with his shipping manifests and my mom with her history curriculums... they wouldn't even know what to do with a break from reality! Reality was their entire world. They were entirely focused on the tangible, the concrete, the day-to-day business of just living and working. And even if you look at the wider family, the relatives out in Ohio or my mother's side from upstate, none of them have ever spent a single day in a psychiatrist's office, at least not to my knowledge. I mean, I think my cousin Greg might have gone to marriage counseling back in the late nineties, but that was strictly about finances and his wife's spending habits, nothing whatsoever to do with losing touch with the world or anything like that.
